text.t: Two strands of DNA wind around each other into the famous double helix.
This piece is 12 base pairs long, slightly more than one full turn of the helix.
Read one strand from end to end and you get the code C G C G A A T T C G C G.
Its sugar and phosphate backbone runs along the outside, with the bases pointing in.
In the middle, adenine on one strand pairs with thymine on the other.
These A and T pairs are propeller twisted, not perfectly flat, which helps the bases stack.
At both ends, guanine pairs with cytosine, held by hydrogen bonds across the middle of the helix.
The helix has a wide major groove and a narrow minor groove.
Proteins read the chemical patterns in these grooves to find their spot without unwinding the DNA.

does.t: DNA is the genetic material of all living things.
Its code is read one base at a time, A, T, C or G, to build proteins.
Each cell in your body carries about 1.5 gigabytes of genetic information.

shape.t: A always pairs with T and G with C, forming a matching set of hydrogen bonds across the helix.
A purine always pairs with a pyrimidine, which keeps the helix the same width all the way along.
Real DNA is not perfectly smooth: this piece is bent by 19 degrees by the way it packs in the crystal.

text.t: In animal and plant cells DNA is kept in the nucleus; in bacteria it sits in a region called the nucleoid.

wrong.t: Chemicals and radiation can damage DNA, and cells build repair proteins to fix the corrupted information.

history.who: H.R. Drew, R.M. Wing, T. Takano, C. Broka, S. Tanaka, K. Itakura and R.E. Dickerson

text.t: Watson and Crick worked out how DNA's base pairs store information in the 1950s.
This 1981 X-ray structure of a synthetic 12 base-pair DNA showed the B form, the shape DNA takes in cells, in atomic detail.

compare.t: This 12 base-pair piece is about 4.4 nm from end to end, and the helix is 2 nm wide.
Each base pair adds 0.34 nm, so one turn of 10 base pairs is 3.4 nm long.
